title: Sketch to ink: the soldering milestone
summary: With an adult at the bench the whole hour: safety brief, ten practice joints on scrap, then the week 1 AND gate soldered permanent on perfboard, a badge they understand down to the last leg.
materials: an adult at the bench for the whole session
soldering iron kit (temperature controlled, stand, lead-free solder, brass tip cleaner)
kid-size safety glasses, two pairs, one for each of you
helping hands or small PCB vise
perfboard, plus a scrap corner cut off it for practice
hookup wire and offcut wire scraps
the week 1 gate parts: 2 buttons, LED, resistor, battery holder with 2 AA batteries
graph paper, pencil and a marker

steps.body: Five minutes on your typing site, and today the words come from the bench. Warm up on the home row, then type the five bench words until your fingers know them: iron, joint, solder, stand, shiny. Finish by typing this sentence three times, fast and clean: the iron lives in my hand or in its stand, never on the table. By the end of today that sentence will be true of your own two hands.

figure.alt: A planned loop drawn before soldering: the red wire leads to Button 1, then Button 2, down into a Resistor, across to an LED with its long leg marked as the entry point, and back to the black wire, forming one closed chain, the same shape as the week 1 AND gate. A note says the drawing must close into a loop or the solder version won't either.

items.s: One dot per hole; if the drawing doesn't close into a loop,

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop, same as always: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: how does a sketch become a thing that lasts? Your week 1 AND gate lived on the breadboard, and a breadboard is a sketch: parts pushed into springy holes, easy to change, easy to lose. Today that circuit gets inked. Solder is ink: melted metal that grips the copper and does not let go. The rule of ink is simple and worth saying out loud: you only ink what you fully understand. You qualify. You built this gate with your own hands, you wrote its truth table, and you can predict all four rows before touching a button.

Imagine: a badge. A small board you can hold up, press with two thumbs, and watch answer a question with a light. Something that still works next year.

Plan: draw the badge on graph paper before the iron warms up. One dot per perfboard hole, every part drawn where it will really sit: button one, button two, resistor, LED with its long leg marked, and the battery holder's red and black wires. Then draw the chain as a line through the drawing: red wire, through button one, through button two, through the resistor, through the LED long leg to short leg, home to the black wire. One loop, exactly like week 1. If the line on paper does not close into a loop, the solder version will not either, and solder is much harder to erase.

steps.title: The safety brief: bench rules
steps.body:
Every real workshop runs on bench rules, and today you learn the soldering set. The rules are not there because you are nine. The adult beside you follows every single one too, every time they solder. Rules are what let a maker relax and do good work next to a tool that melts metal.

The rules, said out loud by both of you before the iron is plugged in:

1. The adult is at the bench the whole time. No solo soldering this season, full stop.
2. Glasses on both faces before the iron gets power. Solder can spit a tiny bead when it meets a damp spot.
3. The iron lives in my hand or in its stand, never on the table. The metal end is treated as hot from the moment it is plugged in until ten minutes after it is unplugged, because a cooling iron looks exactly like a cold one.
4. The helping hands hold the board. Both of my hands hold tools: one the iron, one the solder. Fingers never hold the work, because metal carries heat fast.
5. The little wisp of smoke is flux doing its job. Keep your nose out of it: work at arm's length with a window open or a fan pushing air gently across the bench, and wash hands when the session ends.

And the calm plan for the one thing we plan never to need: if skin ever touches the hot end, straight to cold running water and hold it there a good long while, telling the adult as you go. Not a secret, not a panic. Burns hate cold water and love being told about early.

Say the five rules back in your own words. When the adult nods, plug in the iron and set it to the temperature the kit's instructions give for lead-free solder.

figure.alt: Two soldered joints compared: on the left, a good joint shown as a shiny cone of solder climbing a wire leg on its pad. On the right, a cold joint shown as a dull ball of solder sitting on top of its leg without flowing. Text explains the iron heats the pad and leg together and solder is fed to that hot joint, never melted on the iron tip and wiped on cold metal.

items.s: Cold joint: solder sits on top,
solder is fed to the hot joint, never to the tip
Iron only in hand or stand, never on the table

steps.title: Why you heat the joint, not the solder
steps.body:
Here is the move that separates a real joint from a fake one: the iron heats the metal of the joint, and the solder is fed to the joint, not to the iron.

Solder only grips metal that is hot enough to wet. Wetting means the melted solder stops being a bead and flows out flat, soaking into every tiny scratch in the copper the way water soaks into a paper towel. When you touch the iron's tip to the pad and the part's leg for a second or two, both get hot together. Then solder touched to that hot joint melts instantly and gets pulled into the gap, hugging pad and leg at once. Let it flow, lift the solder away, then the iron, and hold still while it freezes: a shiny little volcano cone climbing the leg. That joint is metal all the way through.

Do it the other way, melting solder on the iron's tip and wiping the blob onto cold metal, and you get a cold joint: a dull grey ball sitting on top of the copper like a raindrop on a waxed car. It looks attached. It is not. It cracks, it wiggles loose, and circuits with cold joints work on Tuesday and die on Thursday.

One more piece of the physics: metal carries heat fast in every direction. That is why the leg you solder gets hot along its whole length, why the helping hands hold the board instead of fingers, and why a big fat part needs an extra beat of heating before the solder will wet it. Heat the joint. Feed the joint. The solder follows the heat, every time.

figure.alt: A copper pad shown with a thin oxide layer forming on it, then an arrow labelled flux pointing to a second copper pad shown bare, where solder can wet the metal. Text gives the melting points: lead-free solder around 217 degrees Celsius versus old leaded solder around 183, and a safety note to keep your face back from the smoke.

items.s: Sharp smoke: face back, window open or fan running

frames.caption: flux arrives at the hot joint
solder can now wet bare copper

steps.title: Flux: the chemistry that makes solder stick
steps.body:
Heat alone will not make solder grip copper. The moment metal meets air, a thin oxide layer forms in seconds, and solder cannot wet an oxide layer at all.

Flux is the chemical fix. It is a mild acid that dissolves that oxide the instant the iron heats it, leaving bare, hungry metal underneath. That is why solder that looked stubborn a second ago suddenly flows once flux touches hot copper.

Most solder wire already has flux hidden inside its core. You have been using it on every joint without seeing it work.

Two numbers matter here. Lead-free solder, the kind in your kit, melts around 217 C. Old leaded solder melted lower, around 183 C, one reason it wets more easily, and one reason it is not what you are using.

Safety: flux gives off a sharp-smelling smoke when it heats. Keep your face back from the joint, and work with a window open or a fan running.

figure.alt: Helping hands clamp a scrap perfboard with a wire leg through a hole. A tinned iron tip touches the pad and leg together while a spool of solder is fed to that same hot joint from the other hand, with a note to count one steamboat, two steamboat before the solder flows into a cone, then check each of ten joints as good or cold.

items.s: Count: one steamboat, two steamboat, then solder flows into a cone
Ten joints, each named good (shiny cone) or cold (dull ball)

steps.title: Practice joints on scrap
steps.body:
Nobody inks on the good page first. Your first joints happen on the scrap corner of perfboard, with offcut wire, where mistakes cost nothing.

First, tin the tip: touch a little solder to the clean hot tip so it gets a bright silver coat, then wipe it through the brass cleaner. A tinned tip carries heat into the joint far better than a dry grey one. Re-wipe and re-tin any time the tip looks dull.

Clamp the scrap board in the helping hands. Push a wire scrap or a spare resistor leg through a hole so a little tail sticks out the copper side. Now the move from the science step, counted out loud: tip touches pad and leg together, one steamboat, two steamboat, feed solder to the joint until it flows into a small cone, solder hand away, iron away, hold still while it freezes.

Make ten joints. After each one, inspect it like a jeweler and say its name out loud: shiny cone climbing the leg, good joint. Dull ball, or solder sitting on top like a droplet, cold joint. When you get a cold one, and you will, fix it the craftsman's way: touch the iron back on until the whole joint remelts, feed a whisker of fresh solder, and let it freeze again. Turning one bad joint into a good one teaches more than five easy ones in a row.
checklist: Glasses on, iron only ever in my hand or its stand, adult at the bench throughout
The tip is tinned and shiny, and I wiped it on the brass whenever it went dull
Ten practice joints made, each one named good or cold out loud after a close look
At least one cold joint reheated with fresh solder until it turned into a good one

figure.alt: The finished badge: a red wire into Button 1, marked with a dot on one of its two joined-pair legs, chaining into Button 2 the same way, then into a Resistor, into the LED's long leg, and out the LED's short leg to the black wire, one loop start to finish. A note says the multimeter should beep from the red wire to the resistor leg only while both buttons are held.

items.s: marker dot = one leg of each joined pair, found by beep
Multimeter beeps from red wire to resistor leg only while both buttons held
Same gate, same truth table as week 1 - now in ink

steps.title: Ink the gate: the badge
steps.body:
Now the real page. One thing changes from the breadboard world: this perfboard has no hidden connections at all. Every hole is its own little island with its own copper pad. Nothing touches anything unless you join it with wire and solder. The whole circuit will be exactly the connections you make, no more and no fewer.

Start with the buttons, and start with the multimeter, because a button still has its secret insides: its four legs come as two joined pairs, the pairs that faced each other across the breadboard's gap, and pressing is what bridges pair to pair. On perfboard you must find the pairs before you solder. Beep mode, probes on two legs at a time, button not pressed: a beep means those two legs are the same pair. Find both pairs on both buttons and put a marker dot on one leg of each pair. The chain must go in through one pair and out through the other, so that the press is the only bridge.

Seat both buttons on the perfboard where your graph paper plan puts them, legs through four holes each, and solder all four legs of each button so they sit strong. Then the resistor, then the LED, minding its one-way rule: long leg is where current goes in, and backwards means dark, not broken. Mark which hole got the long leg. The battery holder's red and black wires go through their holes last and get soldered too.

Now the chain, in hookup wire on the copper side, straight off your plan: red battery wire to a marked leg of button one. Button one's other pair out to a marked leg of button two. Button two's other pair out to one resistor leg. The other resistor leg to the LED's long leg. The LED's short leg to the black battery wire. Five connections, each one stripped, hooked through or laid along the legs, and soldered with the heat-the-joint move.

Before any battery goes in, the multimeter interviews the copper, same as week 1: beep mode, one probe on the red wire's free end, the other on the resistor leg nearest the buttons. Press both buttons: beep. Let go of either one: silence. If it beeps with nothing pressed, a chain wire is riding the same pair on one button, in and out through legs that were already joined, and the press is not in the path: move that wire to the other pair.

Batteries in. Run the four-way interview one more time in this circuit's life: neither, only one, only the other, both. Only both lights it. Hold the badge next to your week 1 truth table and check all four rows. Same gate, same table, but this one is in ink.
checklist: The multimeter found both joined pairs on each button before any soldering, and one leg of each pair got a marker dot
The chain runs in through one pair and out through the other on both buttons, so pressing is the only bridge
With no batteries, the meter beeped from the red wire to the resistor's near leg only while both buttons were held
With batteries in, the LED lights when both buttons are pressed and stays dark the other three ways
Every joint on the board passes the jeweler's look: shiny cones, no dull balls, no solder bridging two neighbour pads

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body: One line per thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. This week's classics: a cold joint that looks attached and is not, found by the jeweler's look or a gentle wiggle with pliers, fixed by reheating with a whisker of fresh solder. A solder bridge, one blob joining two neighbour pads that should be islands, split by dragging the clean hot tip through the gap. The LED in backwards, which means dark, not broken. And the sneakiest: the chain wired in and out through the same joined pair of a button, so the LED ignores that button completely. The multimeter catches that one before the batteries ever do: a beep with nothing pressed means a press is missing from the path. Write down which one got you and how you knew.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the finished badge lit with both thumbs pressing, next to your graph paper plan and the week 1 truth table, plus a close-up of the three joints you are proudest of
